prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I move my preferred configuration to optical lattice clocks. It is a concrete invention in the discovery-or-invention sense the prize requires: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removed Doppler and recoil limits for neutral atoms, and Ye's group took systematic uncertainty to the 10^-18 level. Five members placed it in their top three and several (Kroll, Lindroth, Pearce, Danielsson) independently describe attribution as a clean two-name split. The result has been reproduced in several laboratories, it enables relativistic redshift tests at the millimetre scale and a path to redefining the second, and it is distinct from the comb and ion-trap work prized in 2005 and 2012. I measure it as an experimentalist: the control of lattice light shifts and blackbody effects is exactly the kind of quantitative, reproducible measurement that gives a prize a firm footing.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes on frequency combs (2005) and trapped-ion control (2012), which may make the committee feel that precision metrology has been honoured already. Allocation is also not free of dispute: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others contributed to the first lattice clocks and the 10^-18 milestones, and a two-name credit leaves them out. Finally the SI second has not yet been redefined, so some of the practical consequence is still prospective. Against that, B013 has stronger breadth of impact and equal first-place support, so I do not treat my preference as settled.

responses.point: Ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first: a theoretical flat-band prediction followed by the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity, reproduced by many groups, so recognition is timely rather than premature.
responses.response: I agree on originality and on the prediction-plus-experiment shape, and my own ballot had it fifth, not low. Where I differ is allocation and maturity. The decisive experimental papers were led by Yuan Cao as first author and the three-name cap forces us to leave him and Fatemi out, and we would also be passing over the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto work. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still contested. Reproduction of the phenomenon is solid, but I would want the committee to decide explicitly how it handles the student-led experiment before treating B013 as ready. I regard it as the leading alternative rather than as inferior.

responses.point: Argues that twisted bilayer graphene is a rare case where calculation anticipated a qualitatively new regime and experiment confirmed it, and that a prize could be built from MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero alone.
responses.response: That is the best argument for B013 and I take it seriously. A theory-experiment pair is a defensible shape. But dropping Bistritzer from the pair would sever the very prediction you value, since Bistritzer was first author of the continuum-model paper, and keeping all three means the experimental side is represented by a group leader while the first author is excluded. That tension is what keeps me from putting B013 ahead of a clean case, though I accept that on breadth of impact it is probably larger than clocks.

responses.point: Ranks optical lattice clocks first, judging the magic-wavelength and blackbody-shift physics directly and treating the 2005 comb prize as having left the clock application itself unrecognised.
responses.response: I share this assessment and your point helps me on the overlap objection. The 2005 prize recognised the comb and precision spectroscopy as a tool, not the neutral-atom lattice clock as an invention. I would ask you, as the atomic physicist, how the committee should treat the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow, and whether the 10^-18 milestones belong to Ye alone or to a wider group. If you judge the allocation to Katori and Ye as defensible on that atomic-structure basis, the case is stronger than I could make from my own side of the field.

responses.point: Ranks clocks first and light-matter quantum interfaces second, calling the latter plausible but arguably a few years early and wide in scope with rare-earth-crystal and warm-vapour approaches not represented in the trio.
responses.response: I agree with your caution on B002. I ranked it last on my own ballot for the same reasons: it is a compound field without a single decisive result, and it overlaps with the 2012 and 2022 prizes. Your point about solid-state memories not being represented sharpens the allocation problem. Where I would push back slightly is on the idea that a three-way split is merely non-unique. Because no single milestone defines it, I think it fails the discovery-or-invention test as it stands and should not be a fallback if clocks stall.

responses.point: Ranks Cirac-Zoller quantum computation and simulation theory first, as the conceptual blueprint for ion and atom platforms, with clean two-name credit.
responses.response: I accept that the credit is clean and the impact is large, but I have a qualification: this is a theory prize whose experimental realisation was largely honoured in 2012 and 2022, which is the same overlap concern I raise for clocks, only stronger. The committee would need to explain why proposals rather than the platforms they spawned are the discovery. I also doubt it can share a prize with another achievement without exceeding the three-person limit, so I would treat it as a standalone alternative.

responses.point: Ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy first for opening a new observational window, while acknowledging that source identification is still partial and that large-collaboration allocation is sensitive.
responses.response: I accept the instrumental achievement and the established diffuse flux. My difficulty is attribution. A two-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds is contentious, and your own ballot concedes that source identification is still evolving. Compared with a result where the credit falls naturally on two people, I find B009 harder to resolve fairly. I would want to see whether Danielsson, who also placed it in the top three, can argue for a specific credit rule that resolves the problem.

uncertainties: Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow or others have claims to the lattice-clock credit that make two names unfair.
Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes make the committee judge optical clocks as insufficiently distinct.
Whether Cao and Fatemi on the experimental side of twisted bilayer graphene can be fairly left out, and whether the superconductivity mechanism question affects timing.
Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the SI second redefinition before recognising lattice clocks.
statement.conflict_note: My own B056 (aberration-corrected electron microscopy) sits in my research field of transmission electron microscopy and the international microscopy community where I hold a leadership role, so I should be recused from deciding it and have discounted it in my preferred configuration; I list it only as an alternative for the committee to weigh without my vote. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B061 or B013; the Chalmers connection with Göran Johansson does not touch these candidates.
